h: Deer, crags and a sculpture trail with history
p: Here's a bit of backstory that makes the art even better. The sculpture programme at Grizedale got going back in 1977, which makes it one of the earliest forest art projects of its kind in Britain. Over the decades artists have come and gone, pieces have been added, and some of the older ones have been left to weather back into the woodland on purpose. So don't be surprised if a sculpture looks a bit mossy and battered. That's often the whole point.

Keep your eyes peeled for wildlife as well as artwork. Red deer and roe deer live in the forest, and a quiet walker early or late in the day has the best chance of spotting them. Red squirrels turn up in this corner of Cumbria too, so it's worth having a camera handy.

If you want a view to brag about, the higher ground in the middle of the forest opens out over the fells, with the Coniston range and Windermere in different directions on a clear day. Steady climbing is involved, so it suits older kids and keen walkers more than toddlers in a buggy.

How long to allow? A short family stroll and a bite at the café fits into a couple of hours, but bikers and proper walkers can easily make a full day of it. Arriving early on a sunny weekend or in the school holidays is a smart move, because the car parks do fill.

Want to stretch the day? Hawkshead is home to the Beatrix Potter Gallery, and her old farmhouse, Hill Top, is just down the lanes at Near Sawrey. Tarn Hows, one of the best-loved easy walks in the Lakes, is a short hop away too.
